## Introduction

Every Codespace you have opened arrived identical to every other one. That is the point --- it is what lets every example in these tutorials match your screen.

But *identical for everyone* is not the same as *set up for you*. A machine built from `codespace-starter` knows nothing about you personally, which is why GitHub Advanced ended with two commands you run "once per machine": `gh auth login`, and `git config --global credential.helper store`. Every new Codespace, the same two commands, or `connect-repo` running them for you.

###

This tutorial retires them. A **dotfile** is a configuration file whose name starts with a dot, which is how Unix hides it from an ordinary `ls`. `.bashrc` configures the bash shell. `.gitconfig` configures Git. Today you put yours in a repo that GitHub reads every time it builds you a machine --- and you put the two things that must *not* go in a repo, your GitHub token and your Census API key, where GitHub keeps secrets.

Two things make this tutorial unusual. The repo you make is **permanent**. Every other repo in this course is scratch work, but this one you keep. And you will **not** open it as your workspace. Everything happens in the bash Terminal.

### Exercise 1

In the bash Terminal, run:

```bash
echo $COOLEST_TEACHER
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: introduction-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run echo $COOLEST_TEACHER. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ echo $COOLEST_TEACHER

```

###

Nothing. A blank line, and then your prompt again.

**It did not fail.** Bash treats a variable nobody has set as the empty string, so `echo` printed the empty string and finished happily. Run `echo $?` next and you will get `0`, which is bash for *success*.

By the end of this tutorial, that command will print `Preceptor` on a machine which does not exist yet.

### Exercise 2

In the Antigravity tutorial, the agent stopped to ask permission before most actions. `agy --dangerously-skip-permissions` starts it in a mode that does not ask. That flag is long enough that nobody types it twice, so we will give it a short name, `agyd`. First check that no such name exists yet. In the bash Terminal, run:

```bash
alias agyd
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: introduction-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run alias agyd. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ alias agyd
bash: alias: agyd: not found
```

###

An **alias** is a short name for a longer command, and bash keeps them in memory for the current shell. This one does not exist, and this time bash says so. Aliases live in `.bashrc`, which is where yours will go.

### Exercise 3

`~/.bashrc` runs every time you open a bash Terminal. The starter put several blocks in it. In the bash Terminal, show the one about your prompt:

```bash
grep -A 2 short-prompt ~/.bashrc
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: introduction-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run grep -A 2 short-prompt ~/.bashrc. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ grep -A 2 short-prompt ~/.bashrc
# codespace-starter:short-prompt — short prompt for beginners (folder name + $).
PROMPT_COMMAND=''
PS1='\W \$ '
```

###

There is the reason your prompt says `codespace-starter $` instead of the long one GitHub gives everybody else. `PS1` holds your prompt, and `\W` means *the name of the current directory*, which is why it changes as you `cd` around. (`PROMPT_COMMAND` is cleared first because the stock Codespaces prompt rebuilds itself through it on every render --- clearing it is what lets the simple `PS1` stick.)

`codespace-starter`'s setup script **appends** those lines to the end of `~/.bashrc` while the Codespace is being built, before you ever open a terminal. `.bashrc` already belongs to somebody, and in a few minutes you will add lines after theirs rather than replace the file.

## Your Dotfiles Repo

You need a repo, and you need a way to get files out of it and into your home directory.

### Exercise 1

In the bash Terminal, run `gh auth status`.

If it reports that you are **not** logged in, run the sign-in ritual from GitHub Advanced and then run `gh auth status` again:

```bash
unset GITHUB_TOKEN GH_TOKEN
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false
git config --global credential.helper store
printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\n' "$(gh auth token)" > ~/.git-credentials
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run gh auth status. If it reports that you are not logged in, run the sign-in ritual from GitHub Advanced (unset GITHUB_TOKEN GH_TOKEN, then gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web --clipboard=false, then git config --global credential.helper store, then printf 'https://x-access-token:%s@github.com\\n' \"$(gh auth token)\" > ~/.git-credentials) and then run gh auth status again. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ gh auth status
github.com
  ✓ Logged in to github.com account your-username (/home/rstudio/.config/gh/hosts.yml)
  - Active account: true
  - Git operations protocol: https
  - Token: gho_************************************
  - Token scopes: 'gist', 'read:org', 'repo', 'workflow'
```

###

The login lives in `hosts.yml`, inside this one Codespace. A fresh Codespace is logged out, which is why every tutorial so far has started with `connect-repo` or with these four commands.

### Exercise 2

Make the repo. In the bash Terminal:

```bash
cd /workspaces
gh repo create dotfiles --private --clone
cd dotfiles
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run cd /workspaces, then gh repo create dotfiles --private --clone, then cd dotfiles. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",

```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ cd /workspaces
workspaces $ gh repo create dotfiles --private --clone
✓ Created repository your-username/dotfiles on GitHub
  https://github.com/your-username/dotfiles
✓ Initialized repository in "/workspaces/dotfiles"
workspaces $ cd dotfiles
dotfiles $
```

###

The same command you used for `scratch-repo` and `github-advanced`, with one difference. GitHub reads this repo using your own permissions, so a private one works exactly as well as a public one, and there is no reason to publish your settings to the world.

The name is a convention, not a rule. GitHub lets you pick any repo you own from a dropdown, but essentially every dotfiles repo you will ever meet is called `dotfiles`, so ours is too.

### Exercise 3

GitHub sets up your machine in one of two ways, and you pick by what you put in the repo. If it finds an **install script** --- `install.sh` is the first name it looks for --- it runs that and stops. If there is no install script, it instead **symlinks** every dotted file in the repo into your home directory.

Use a script, and keep it tiny. Ask AI to create three files in `/workspaces/dotfiles`.

First, `install.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -e
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

cat bashrc >> ~/.bashrc
cat gitconfig >> ~/.gitconfig
```

Second, `bashrc`, two lines:

```bash
export COOLEST_TEACHER=Preceptor
alias agyd='agy --dangerously-skip-permissions'
```

Third, `gitconfig`, with your real name and your own GitHub username:

```ini
[user]
	name = Your Name
	email = YOUR-USERNAME@users.noreply.github.com
[init]
	defaultBranch = main
[alias]
	s = status --short --branch
	l = log --oneline --graph --decorate -20
[credential]
	helper =
	helper = !gh auth git-credential
```

In the bash Terminal, run `cat /workspaces/dotfiles/gitconfig`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Ask AI to create install.sh, bashrc, and gitconfig in /workspaces/dotfiles with the contents shown. In the bash Terminal, run cat /workspaces/dotfiles/gitconfig. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
[user]
	name = David Kane
	email = your-username@users.noreply.github.com
[init]
	defaultBranch = main
[alias]
	s = status --short --branch
	l = log --oneline --graph --decorate -20
[credential]
	helper =
	helper = !gh auth git-credential
```

###

Neither `bashrc` nor `gitconfig` has a leading dot, and that is deliberate. They are **fragments** to be appended to files that already exist, not files to be installed. If you ever delete `install.sh`, GitHub falls back to symlinking, and a file named `.gitconfig` in this repo would then replace the real one.

`[user]` is the part that matters. Git refuses to commit until it knows who you are, and outside a Codespace --- on your laptop, say --- a fresh machine does not. Use the `@users.noreply.github.com` address rather than your real one. Your commits carry that email into every public repo you ever push to, and published email addresses get scraped.

In the `[credential]` block, the first `helper =` line, with nothing after the equals sign, clears whatever credential helpers the machine came with. The second tells Git to ask `gh` for a password whenever it needs one.

The `alias` line in `bashrc` means that typing `agyd` runs `agy --dangerously-skip-permissions`. An agent that never asks permission is fine in a disposable Codespace holding work that is already on GitHub. Do not use it on a machine you care about.

###

Two characters in `install.sh` do more work than the rest of the file.

`>>` **appends** to a file. A single `>` would overwrite it.

Most dotfiles repos on the internet contain a whole `.bashrc`. With no install script, GitHub would symlink theirs straight over the top of the one you looked at in the Introduction. Your prompt would become GitHub's long default in every Codespace you ever opened, and every example in these tutorials would stop matching your screen.

The rule generalises: **when you do not own a file, add to it rather than replace it.** Ask AI to change your shell configuration and it will hand you a complete `.bashrc`. Append the lines you need instead.

(`set -e` means stop at the first command that fails. `cd "$(dirname "$0")"` moves to wherever the script happens to live, since you do not know what directory GitHub will run it from.)

### Exercise 4

GitHub runs the script only if it is executable. In the bash Terminal, make it so:

```bash
chmod +x install.sh
```

Then run `ls -l install.sh`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run chmod +x install.sh, then ls -l install.sh. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
dotfiles $ ls -l install.sh
-rwxr-xr-x 1 rstudio rstudio 95 Oct 23 14:22 install.sh
```

###

The `x` characters in `-rwxr-xr-x` are the **executable bit**. Before `chmod +x` the line read `-rw-r--r--` and the file was just text that happened to contain commands.

A missing executable bit is the most common way a dotfiles repo silently does nothing. The script is there, GitHub declines to run it, and no error appears anywhere. Git stores this bit, which is why it survives the trip to a new machine.

### Exercise 5

Commit all three files with the message `Add install script and fragments`, and push. This is a brand-new repo, so the first push is `git push -u origin main`, as in GitHub Advanced. Then, in the bash Terminal, run `git log --oneline`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: repo-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Commit all three files with the message \"Add install script and fragments\" and push with git push -u origin main. In the bash Terminal, run git log --oneline. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
dotfiles $ git log --oneline
4c1e2a9 (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Add install script and fragments
```

###

`origin/main` on the same line as `HEAD -> main` is the proof that the push landed. GitHub reads this repo from *its* servers when it builds a machine, not from your Codespace, so a commit that is only local does nothing.

## What Does Not Belong In A Repo

Everything in `gitconfig` is a **setting**: true for years, and harmless if the whole world read it. Your GitHub token is neither. It is a password, and a password in a repo --- even a private one --- is a copy on GitHub, a copy on every machine you ever open, and a line in Git history that outlives every attempt to delete it.

GitHub keeps a separate place for values like that, and it delivers them the same way: when a Codespace is created.

### Exercise 1

Make a token. Go to <https://github.com/settings/tokens/new?scopes=repo,read:org,workflow&description=Codespaces>. The note and the three scopes are already filled in. Set **Expiration** to a date after the end of this course, then click **Generate token**.

GitHub shows the token once, on the next page. Copy it somewhere safe for the next exercise. **Never paste the token itself into this tutorial, or anywhere else that is saved.**

Then go to <https://github.com/settings/tokens> and take a screenshot of the token list, which shows the new token's name and expiration but never its value, and paste it below. To take a screenshot, press `Cmd + Ctrl + Shift + 4` on a Mac, `Win + Shift + S` on Windows, or `Ctrl + Shift + Show windows` on a Chromebook, select the area, then click in the answer box and press `Cmd + V` (Mac) or `Ctrl + V` (Windows) to paste it.

```{r}
#| label: secrets-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Create a classic personal access token at github.com/settings/tokens/new with the repo, read:org, and workflow scopes and an expiration after the end of the course. Copy it somewhere safe. Then take a screenshot of the token list at github.com/settings/tokens, showing the new token's name and expiration, and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your screenshot should show a token named `Codespaces` with its expiration date, and nothing that starts with `ghp_`.

###

Those three scopes --- `repo`, `read:org`, `workflow` --- are the same ones `gh auth login` asked for in GitHub Advanced. A token is a password with a job description attached: this one can read and write your repositories and nothing else about your account.

A leaked token works until someone revokes it. An expiry date revokes it whether you remember to or not.

### Exercise 2

You already own a second key. In the census tutorial you ran `census_api_key("...", install = TRUE)`, which wrote your Census API key into `~/.Renviron`. Count its lines without showing the key. In the bash Terminal, run:

```bash
grep -c CENSUS ~/.Renviron
```

CP/CR.

If it prints `0`, or says the file does not exist, you do not have a key yet. Sign up for a free one at <https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html>, click the activation link in the email, and keep the key for the next exercise.

```{r}
#| label: secrets-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run grep -c CENSUS ~/.Renviron. CP/CR. If it prints 0 or says the file does not exist, sign up for a free key at https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html, click the activation link in the email, and keep the key for the next exercise.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ grep -c CENSUS ~/.Renviron
1
```

###

`-c` counts matching lines instead of printing them, which keeps the key off your screen. `~/.Renviron` is a file R reads when it starts, and it exists on this machine only. A new Codespace has no such file, which is why `get_acs()` would fail there until you installed the key again.

### Exercise 3

Go to <https://github.com/settings/codespaces>. Under **Codespaces secrets**, click **New secret**. Name it `GH_TOKEN`, paste your token as the value, and under **Repository access** select `PPBDS/codespace-starter`. Add it.

Then add a second secret the same way, named `CENSUS_API_KEY`, with your Census key as the value and the same repository access. The key is the text after `CENSUS_API_KEY=` in `~/.Renviron`. In the bash Terminal, `code ~/.Renviron` opens the file so you can copy it.

Take a screenshot of the **Codespaces secrets** list showing both secrets and the repository they can reach, and paste it below. The list shows names only, never the values, so the screenshot is safe to submit.

```{r}
#| label: secrets-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "At github.com/settings/codespaces, add a Codespaces secret named GH_TOKEN with your token as the value and PPBDS/codespace-starter under Repository access. Then add a second secret named CENSUS_API_KEY with your Census key as the value and the same repository access (the key is the text after CENSUS_API_KEY= in ~/.Renviron; code ~/.Renviron opens the file). Take a screenshot of the Codespaces secrets list showing both secrets and the repository they can reach, and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your screenshot should show two secrets, `CENSUS_API_KEY` and `GH_TOKEN`, each with `PPBDS/codespace-starter` under its repository access.

###

`GH_TOKEN` is the name `gh` looks for. `gh` prefers it over the `GITHUB_TOKEN` that GitHub puts into every Codespace, the built-in token that can only touch `codespace-starter` and cannot create repos, which is why `connect-repo` starts by unsetting it. With `GH_TOKEN` in the environment, `gh` acts as you, and so does `git`, because the `[credential]` lines in your `gitconfig` tell it to ask `gh`.

`CENSUS_API_KEY` is the name **tidycensus** looks for. A Codespaces secret arrives as an environment variable, and every process on the machine sees it, including the R Terminal, `Rscript`, and `quarto render`. So `get_acs()` finds the key with no `.Renviron` at all. `install = TRUE` remains the right way on a laptop, where there is no secret store.

You picked `codespace-starter` because that is the repo your Codespaces are built from. The secrets go to machines made from that repo, whatever repo you then create inside them.

###

Two boxes on one settings page, for two different kinds of thing.

- **Dotfiles** deliver *files you wrote* by cloning your repo onto the machine: your name, your `agyd` alias, your prompt. Settings. Things you want to keep forever and would not mind anyone reading.
- **Secrets** deliver *values GitHub holds encrypted*, straight into the environment, with nothing written to disk or to any repo. Your GitHub token, your Census key. Things you may one day need to revoke in a hurry.

When you are not sure which box something belongs in, ask whether a leak would embarrass you or get you *in trouble*. Embarrassed is a dotfile. In trouble is a secret.

## Turning It On

The repo exists, and so far it does nothing. GitHub will not go looking for it until you say so. The switch is not in the repo but in your account, on the page you just left.

Go back to <https://github.com/settings/codespaces>.

Under **Dotfiles**, tick **Automatically install dotfiles**, and use the dropdown to choose your `dotfiles` repository.

Take a screenshot of the **Dotfiles** section, showing the ticked box and the repository you chose, and paste it below.

Both switches on this page are **account** settings, not repo settings: from here on they apply to every Codespace you create, in any repo, in any organisation, whether you own that repo or not.

###

Check the bash Terminal you are sitting in: `$COOLEST_TEACHER` is still empty, and it will stay empty here no matter how long you wait.

Dotfiles and secrets are delivered when a Codespace is created. This one was created before you had either, and nothing goes back to revisit it. **Settings that apply at creation do not reach a machine that already exists.** The only way to see any of this work is to build a new machine.

### Exercise 3

Still in the **new** Codespace, in its bash Terminal, run:

```bash
gh auth status
git config --get user.name

tail -2 ~/.bashrc
```

CP/CR back here.

```{r}

#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Still in the new Codespace, in its bash Terminal, run gh auth status, then git config --get user.name, then alias agyd, then tail -2 ~/.bashrc. CP/CR back here.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
codespace-starter $ gh auth status
github.com
  ✓ Logged in to github.com account your-username (GH_TOKEN)
  - Active account: true
  - Git operations protocol: https
  - Token: ghp_************************************
  - Token scopes: 'read:org', 'repo', 'workflow'
codespace-starter $ git config --get user.name
David Kane
codespace-starter $ alias agyd
alias agyd='agy --dangerously-skip-permissions'
codespace-starter $ tail -2 ~/.bashrc
export COOLEST_TEACHER=Preceptor
alias agyd='agy --dangerously-skip-permissions'
```

###

You are signed in as yourself on a brand new machine. Not through `hosts.yml`, which does not exist here, and not as the Codespace's built-in token, which `gh` would report as `(GITHUB_TOKEN)`, but through the secret, which `gh` reports as `(GH_TOKEN)`. Git knows your name because `install.sh` appended your `gitconfig`, so you can create a repo and commit to it without Git stopping to ask.

`agyd` exists now, and the last two lines of `.bashrc` are yours. The starter's lines went in while the Codespace was being built, your `install.sh` ran when it was created, and `>>` put your lines after theirs. The starter's `PS1` survived, which is why your prompt still reads `codespace-starter $`. Had you shipped a whole `.bashrc` with no install script, it would not have.

Other things belong in the same repo: a `.gitignore_global` so junk files never reach a repo again, more aliases, R options. Anything you would otherwise redo on every machine.

###

Codespaces are billed by the hour, and two running machines burn your allowance twice as fast.

Deleting it cost you nothing. Everything that made that machine yours was on GitHub, a repo and two secrets, not on the machine. The computer is disposable, and nothing important lives only there.

## Summary

You started with `echo $COOLEST_TEACHER` printing nothing --- successfully, because an unset variable in bash is empty rather than broken. You finished with the same command printing `Preceptor` on a machine that did not exist when you began, and with that machine already signed in to GitHub as you.

###

In between you built a private repo called `dotfiles` holding an executable `install.sh` and two fragments, `bashrc` and `gitconfig`, which the script **appends** to the real files rather than replacing them. The fragments carry your Git identity, your aliases, and `agyd`. You put the two things that must not live in a repo, your GitHub token and your Census API key, in the Codespaces secrets `GH_TOKEN` and `CENSUS_API_KEY`. And you flipped the account-level switches that deliver all of it to every Codespace you create from now on.

###

From here on, a tutorial that says *create a repo called `whatever` and connect to it* needs no login step and no `connect-repo`:

```bash
cd /workspaces
gh repo create whatever --public --clone
cd whatever
```

Then **File -> Open Folder...** on `/workspaces/whatever`, as always. `connect-repo` still works if you prefer it --- it also drops an `AGENTS.md` into the repo and makes new terminals open there --- but it no longer has anything to log you in to.

###

One rule to carry forward: **settings that apply at creation do not reach a machine that already exists.** Dotfiles and secrets alike.
